title: Gyroscopic Effects: Vector Aspects of Angular Momentum
lead: Angular momentum has a direction as well as a size, and this section is about that direction. The right-hand rule gives it: curl the fingers of your right hand the way a body turns, and your thumb points along its angular velocity and its angular momentum. A torque changes angular momentum in the torque's own direction, so a torque perpendicular to the angular momentum swings the axis of rotation sideways rather than tipping it over. That is why a spinning bicycle wheel turns toward the person who tries to tip it, why a gyroscope precesses instead of falling, and why Earth's axis sweeps slowly round the sky once in about 26,000 years.
objectives: Describe the right-hand rule to find the direction of angular velocity, momentum, and torque.
Study how Earth acts like a gigantic gyroscope.
summary_html:
• Torque is perpendicular to the plane formed by $r$ and $\kF$ and is the direction your right thumb would point if you curled the fingers of your right hand in the direction of $\kF$. The direction of the torque is thus the same as that of the angular momentum it produces.
  • The gyroscope precesses around a vertical axis, since the torque is always horizontal and perpendicular to $\kL$. If the gyroscope is not spinning, it acquires angular momentum in the direction of the torque ($\kL = \kdLang$), and it rotates about a horizontal axis, falling over just as we would expect.
  • Earth itself acts like a gigantic gyroscope. Its angular momentum is along its axis and points at Polaris, the North Star.

figures.original_caption: Figure (a) shows a disk is rotating counterclockwise when viewed from above. Figure (b) shows the right-hand rule. The direction of angular velocity ω size and angular momentum L are defined to be the direction in which the thumb of your right hand points when you curl your fingers in the direction of the disk’s rotation as shown.

In figure (a), the torque is perpendicular to the plane formed by r and F and is the direction your right thumb would point to if you curled your fingers in the direction of F. Figure (b) shows that the direction of the torque is the same as that of the angular momentum it produces.

In figure (a), a person holding the spinning bike wheel lifts it with her right hand and pushes down with her left hand in an attempt to rotate the wheel. This action creates a torque directly toward her. This torque causes a change in angular momentum ΔL in exactly the same direction. Figure (b) shows a vector diagram depicting how ΔL and L add, producing a new angular momentum pointing more toward the person. The wheel moves toward the person, perpendicular to the forces she exerts on it.

As seen in figure (a), the forces on a spinning gyroscope are its weight and the supporting force from the stand. These forces create a horizontal torque on the gyroscope, which create a change in angular momentum ΔL that is also horizontal. In figure (b), ΔL and L add to produce a new angular momentum with the same magnitude, but different direction, so that the gyroscope precesses in the direction shown instead of falling over.

exercises.prompt: Rotational kinetic energy is associated with angular momentum? Does that mean that rotational kinetic energy is a vector?

answer.solution: No, energy is always a scalar whether motion is involved or not. No form of energy has a direction in space and you can see that rotational kinetic energy does not depend on the direction of motion just as linear kinetic energy is independent of the direction of motion.

exercises.prompt: A globe (model of the Earth) is a hollow sphere with a radius of 16 cm. By wrapping a cord around the equator of a globe and pulling on it, a person exerts a torque on the globe of 120 N · m for 1.2 s. What angular momentum does the globe have after 1.2 s?

answer.hint: The globe starts at rest, so the angular momentum it ends with is the whole change, and $\text{net}\;\ktau = \kdLang / \kdt$ gives that change as the torque times the time it acts. The radius of the globe is not needed.
answer.solution: Since the globe is stationary to start with, $\ktau = \frac{\kdLang}{\kdt}$, so $\ktau \cdot \kdt = \kdLang$. By substituting, $120\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m} \cdot 1.2\ \text{s} = 144\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s}$. The angular momentum of the globe after 1.2 s is $144\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s}$.

exercises.prompt: How could you use a fishing reel to test the relationship between the torque applied to a system, the time for which the torque was applied, and the resulting angular momentum of the system? How would you measure angular momentum?

answer.solution: Hang a known mass from the fishing line so that the line pulls on the rim of the spool. The weight of the mass is then the force, the radius of the spool is its lever arm, and their product is the torque on the reel, which stays the same for as long as the mass hangs freely. Release the reel, let the mass pull for a measured time, and then catch the line so that the torque stops. To find the angular momentum the reel has gained, time how long the spool takes to turn through a counted number of revolutions just after the torque stops, which gives its angular velocity, and multiply by the moment of inertia of the spool, which you can estimate from its mass and radius by treating it as a disk or as a hollow cylinder from Figure 10.12. Repeat with the mass pulling for twice and three times as long, and then with twice the mass for the same time, and compare the angular momentum you measure with the product $\ktau\,\kdt$ in each case. The relationship $\text{net}\;\ktau = \kdLang / \kdt$ predicts that the angular momentum grows in step with the time and with the torque, and that a doubled torque acting for half the time leaves the reel with the same angular momentum.

exercises.prompt: While driving his motorcycle at highway speed, a physics student notices that pulling back lightly on the right handlebar tips the cycle to the left and produces a left turn. Explain why this happens.

answer.solution: The front wheel of the motorcycle is a spinning wheel with a large angular momentum, and at highway speed that angular momentum points along the axle, to the rider's left by the right-hand rule. Pulling back on the right handlebar tries to turn the front wheel to the right about a vertical axis, and the torque of that pull is vertical, perpendicular to the angular momentum of the wheel. As with the bicycle wheel in Figure 10.39, the change in angular momentum $\kdLang$ points along the torque, so the axle does not swing to the right as the rider might expect; instead the tip of $\kL$ moves in the direction of the torque and the wheel tilts about a horizontal axis, leaning the motorcycle to the left. Once the motorcycle leans left, its weight and the forces at the tires turn it to the left, which is the turn the student notices. This is the gyroscopic effect of Figure 10.40 at work: the torque changes the direction of the angular momentum, and it does so in its own direction, perpendicular to the way the rider pushes.

exercises.prompt: Gyroscopes used in guidance systems to indicate directions in space must have an angular momentum that does not change in direction. Yet they are often subjected to large forces and accelerations. How can the direction of their angular momentum be constant when they are accelerated?

answer.solution: The direction of an angular momentum changes only when a torque acts on the spinning body, since $\text{net}\;\ktau = \kdLang / \kdt$, and a force by itself is not a torque. A force applied at the center of mass of the gyroscope, or a support that acts through its center of mass, has no lever arm and so exerts no torque, however large the force. A guidance gyroscope is therefore mounted in gimbals, a set of rings that let the frame around it turn freely about every axis, so that the vehicle can pitch, roll and accelerate while the mount passes on only forces through the center of the spinning wheel and no torque about it. With no torque there is no $\kdLang$, the angular momentum keeps its direction in space, and the axle keeps pointing the way it was set no matter how the vehicle around it moves. A large spin helps too: the larger $\kL$ is, the smaller the angle through which any stray torque can swing it in a given time.

At the heads of the two vectors there is a circular shape, directed in counter clockwise direction. An angular momentum vector, directed toward left, along its diameter, is shown. The plane of the Earth’s orbit is shown as a horizontal line through its center.

exercises.prompt: The axis of Earth makes a 23.5° angle with a direction perpendicular to the plane of Earth’s orbit. As shown in Figure 10.41, this axis precesses, making one complete rotation in 25,780 y. (a) Calculate the change in angular momentum in half this time. (b) What is the average torque producing this change in angular momentum? (c) If this torque were created by a single force (it is not) acting at the most effective point on the equator, what would its magnitude be?

parts.hint: Earth's angular momentum is $\kL = \kI\kw$ with the moment of inertia of a solid sphere, $\frac{2}{5}MR^2$, and the angular velocity of one turn a day. In half a precession the axis has swung to the opposite side of the cone, so $\kdLang$ is the third side of a triangle with two sides $\kL$ that meet at $2 \times 23.5^\circ$.
The average torque is $\kdLang / \kdt$, with $\kdt$ half of 25,780 years written in seconds.
The most effective point is where the lever arm is a full Earth radius and the force is perpendicular to it, so the force is the torque divided by $R$.
